title: Treat AI like a brilliant freelancer with amnesia · hancrafted
description: Name the five traits that make AI costly (PRICE), and manage them with five moves (BRIEF): break it down, requirements first, interview yourself with AI, evaluate each step, and a fresh start for each piece.

The thought experiment No speaker notes for this Slide.

You're the new hire Why the middle zone stays unwritten Nonaka calls this tacit knowledge: "highly personal", "hard to formalize and, therefore, difficult to communicate to others"; in Polanyi's words, "We can know more than we can tell" 1 . Sources (1) Ikujiro Nonaka, The Knowledge-Creating Company, Harvard Business Review (Nov-Dec 1991; reprinted as an HBR Classic, Jul-Aug 2007) ( opens in a new tab ) hbr.org The newcomer has the least to absorb with in 122 best-practice transfers between units in eight companies, knowledge-related barriers outweighed motivational ones; the recipient's lack of absorptive capacity weighed most (0.54), ahead of causal ambiguity (0.34) 1 . Sources (1) Gabriel Szulanski, Exploring Internal Stickiness: Impediments to the Transfer of Best Practice Within the Firm, Strategic Management Journal 17 (1996) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Even the experts cannot always say it a master baker's technique could not be read off X-rays of the dough; it took a developer's apprenticeship ("observation, imitation, and practice") and a year of trial and error before it was specified 1 . Sources (1) Ikujiro Nonaka, The Knowledge-Creating Company, Harvard Business Review (Nov-Dec 1991; reprinted as an HBR Classic, Jul-Aug 2007) ( opens in a new tab ) hbr.org One caution on the theory Gourlay disputes Nonaka's account of knowledge being created by converting between tacit and explicit forms; the claim here rests on the definition of tacit knowledge, not on that conversion model 1 . Sources (1) Stephen Gourlay, Conceptualizing Knowledge Creation: A Critique of Nonaka's Theory, Journal of Management Studies 43(7) (2006) ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org

Five traits, or you pay the price Right or not, the output looks finished even state-of-the-art models "still regularly produce logical mistakes", which is why speed without checking is a trap 1 . Sources (1) Lightman et al., Let's Verify Step by Step ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Probable, not random text generation samples from a probability distribution rather than always picking the single likeliest word, because the always-likeliest text is bland and repetitive 1 . Even with randomness set to zero the provider documents that "the results will not be fully deterministic" 2 . Sources (2) Holtzman et al., The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Anthropic, Messages API reference (temperature parameter) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com How much varies in one test 1,000 completions of one prompt at zero randomness gave 80 unique answers 1 . Across five models set up for determinism, accuracy moved by up to 15% between runs of the same task 2 . Sources (2) He et al., Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference ( opens in a new tab ) thinkingmachines.ai Atil et al., Non-Determinism of "Deterministic" LLM Settings ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org The bill covers the whole chat the interface is stateless: the earlier turns go in with every request, and the model's own answers become part of the next input 1 . Each resent word is billed as input 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Context windows ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Anthropic, Pricing ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com A discount, not an exemption cached reads cost about a tenth of base input, the default cache lasts 5 minutes, and caching changes what is paid, not whether the words count toward the window 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Prompt caching ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Why it guesses instead of asking most benchmarks score a guess above an abstention, so training rewards guessing 1 . Current models rarely ask for clarification and answer wrongly instead 2 . Sources (2) Kalai et al., Why Language Models Hallucinate ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Kuhn et al., CLAM: Selective Clarification for Ambiguous Questions with Generative Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Why it is blind to your company a model's accuracy on a fact relates to how many documents about it it saw in training 1 , and a leading model family was trained on publicly available data alone 2 . The provider states it does not train on commercial inputs and outputs by default 3 . Sources (3) Kandpal et al., Large Language Models Struggle to Learn Long-Tail Knowledge ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Touvron et al., LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Anthropic, Is my data used for model training? (commercial products) ( opens in a new tab ) privacy.claude.com The forgetting is in the design the context window is described as the model's "working memory", distinct from the corpus it was trained on 1 . Memory across chats exists only where an application stores notes and puts them back, since the memory tool runs client-side 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Context windows ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Anthropic, Memory tool ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

Brief the venue Why the sign-off is a gate Stating every requirement at once is not free: one requirement stated alone was followed 98.7% of the time, but with 19 stated gpt-4o fell to 85.0%, part of it from conflicts between requirements 1 . A short card of essentials is the reason. Sources (1) Yang, Shi, Ma, Liu, Kästner, Wu, What Prompts Don't Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts (v3) ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org A wrong early guess sticks When instructions were revealed piece by piece, models scored 39% lower on average, mostly as unreliability; they “make assumptions in early turns” and do not recover from a wrong turn 1 . Sources (1) Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville, LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Focus beats volume On a long-memory benchmark, prompts holding only the relevant material, only a few hundred words of relevant material scored significantly higher than full prompts of tens of thousands of words, and even a single distractor lowered results 1 . Sources (1) Hong, Troynikov, Huber, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance ( opens in a new tab ) trychroma.com Plan, then fresh session After interviewing for a spec, the vendor's own guidance is to “start a fresh session to execute it”, since the new session “has clean context focused entirely on implementation” 1 . Sources (1) Anthropic, Best practices for Claude Code ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com The answer can be right and the work wrong Among solutions with a correct final answer, the best system cut reasoning errors from 14.0% to 3.4%, so a check on the result alone accepts flawed reasoning 1 . Sources (1) Uesato et al., Solving math word problems with process- and outcome-based feedback ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

How to manage the PRICE Break it down Least-to-most prompting, solving simpler subproblems in sequence, scored 99% or better on a compositional benchmark against 16% for chain-of-thought prompting with an older model 1 . Models can answer every sub-question and still fail the whole one, and that gap does not shrink as models grow 2 . Sources (2) Zhou et al., Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Press et al., Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Requirements first Across prompts that each stated a different subset of 20 requirements, results varied more than twice as much for a requirement left unstated as for one stated: standard deviation 8.9% against under half that 1 . Sources (1) Yang, Shi, Ma, Liu, Kästner, Wu, What Prompts Don't Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts (v3) ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Interview yourself with AI Agents that interacted with the user to fill missing information improved performance by up to 74% on an underspecified coding benchmark 1 . When a model elicits preferences with open-ended questions, users' answers were often more informative than prompts they wrote unaided 2 . Sources (2) Vijayvargiya et al., Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Li et al., Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Evaluate each step On a maths benchmark, feedback on each reasoning step "significantly outperforms" feedback on the final result alone 1 . Models also "struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback", so the check needs something outside the model, here the requirements 2 . Sources (2) Lightman et al., Let's Verify Step by Step ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Huang et al., Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Fresh start for each piece Across six generation tasks, top models scored on average 39% lower in multi-turn conversation than with the full instruction at once; the authors advise starting a new conversation that repeats the information 1 . Performance also degrades with input length across all 18 models tested 2 . Sources (2) Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville, LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org Hong, Troynikov, Huber, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance ( opens in a new tab ) trychroma.com A limit on Break it down Decomposition does not make a model reliable at composing the pieces; errors in early steps still carry into later ones, which is why the next move is checking 1 . Sources (1) Dziri et al., Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

script.text: 0:00 – 0:19 Welcome Welcome to hancrafted. Today's episode is about why you should treat AI like a brilliant freelancer with amnesia. The goal: a fresh perspective, so the next time AI leaves you confused or disappointed, you have a mental model to solve it. Let's get going.
The thought experiment 0:00 – 0:07 The setup Before we start with AI, I want to ground you with a thought experiment. Here's the setup.

You're the new hire 0:00 – 0:19 Obvious questions Imagine you're a new hire. On day one, you get your first task: plan next year's summer party for all 200 employees across Europe. Your first questions are probably: what's the budget, where does everybody stay, who signs off? Maybe even dietary and accessibility needs. 0:19 – 0:37 The ones you forget But the hard questions, the ones people usually don't think of but that matter just as much, are these: what went wrong last time, which unwritten rules apply (no paintball, for example), and which tools and suppliers are you allowed to use? 0:37 – 1:04 Switch of roles Now let's switch roles. You're the one handing this task to a new hire on their first day. It's Monday, and the plan is due Friday. After everything we just went through, I think you realise you need to onboard that person with this context and these limitations, so they can work on it independently without knocking on your door every few minutes.

Five traits, or you pay the price 0:00 – 0:09 Who gets the job Now imagine you hand this job to a freelancer: brilliant, but with amnesia. And they come with five weird traits. 0:09 – 0:24 Probabilistic, Relentless One: they're probabilistic. Ask them the same question twice, and you get a slightly different answer, sometimes a very different one. Two: they're relentless. No bathroom breaks, no sleep, fully locked on whatever task you give them. 0:24 – 0:35 Informed Three: they're very informed. A degree in every subject you can imagine. But they know nothing about you, your company, your culture or your processes. 0:35 – 0:48 Confident, Every word billed Four: they're extremely confident, to the point that they'll sell you their answer as correct. Five: they bill you for every word they hear from you, and every word they say.

What happens with one prompt 0:00 – 0:12 One prompt in So what happens if you just hand them one prompt: plan next year's summer party for 200 employees across Europe? You get a plan. A polished one. Look closer. 0:12 – 0:19 Probabilistic They're probabilistic: ask again, and you get a whole new plan, in Lisbon instead of Berlin. 0:19 – 0:29 Relentless They're relentless: they compared hotels in twelve cities by rating, never asked where your people travel from, and buried you in documents. 0:29 – 0:36 Informed They're informed: they know a thousand team-building activities, and they picked paintball, because they don't know your culture. 0:36 – 0:42 Confident They're confident: the venue prices look like facts, and they're made up. 0:42 – 0:47 Every word billed And they bill per word: you paid for every page of it. 0:47 – 1:03 You saw the AI You've probably noticed: behind every trait, you already saw the AI. But let's stay in the thought experiment. If this were a human freelancer with these five traits, how would you onboard them for a complex task like this? 1:03 – 1:24 The mental model That's the mental model I want to give you. As we go on, you'll see an AI agent behaves, weirdly, in many ways like this brilliant freelancer with amnesia. And your job is to onboard and manage them, so they deliver a result you can work with.

How do we work with this freelancer? 0:00 – 0:12 Answer to the traits Five traits cost you. The good news is that you can answer each of them, with five moves, and the first letters spell BRIEF. That is the second cornerstone.

Brief the venue 0:00 – 0:17 Restate The task: plan the summer party for 200 people across Europe. If you asked AI for all of that in one prompt, you would get pages of polished and confident answers, and you could trust almost none of them. 0:17 – 0:34 Break it down So first, break it down. The party falls into five pieces: venue, travel, catering, invitations and budget. We take only the venue now, and the other four wait for their turn, because one piece is small enough to get right. 0:34 – 0:56 Interview Next, the interview. Before it starts, the AI asks you questions, the way a contact at an agency would. Three questions come up, and one of them is something you had forgotten: whether last year's party left feedback worth keeping. That is the unwritten context coming out before the AI guesses. 0:56 – 1:16 Requirements Then requirements, and this is a stage you sign off before any research starts. Everything gets written onto one card, short and made of essentials, and every later job reads from it. If the card is wrong, you want to find out here, while it is cheap. 1:16 – 1:31 Research, fresh each time Now the research. Three venues get three fresh chats, and each one is checked against the card. Handing work to several of them at once is its own topic, and it is the promotion Episode. 1:31 – 1:47 Compare and check The three results come back together and are compared, again against the card, not against a feeling. That makes two gates in the whole flow: the card, and the comparison. A mistake has to get past both. 1:47 – 2:06 Recommendation, and on What comes out is the venue plan for your boss, and the whole thing ran on the same BRIEF you would use for any task. (pause) Now let's do it live: I will show you how that interview feels when you run it yourself.

How to manage the PRICE 0:00 – 0:36 Recap So, what did we just do? Five moves, in two phases. First, planning. One: let the AI interview you about what you need, your constraints and your ideas. Two: turn that into requirements before you hand over any goal. Three: break the plan down into small pieces. Then, doing. Four: hand each piece to an agent and review every result, because they will sound confident either way. Five: start each piece fresh, in a new conversation, because they bill you for every word.
